extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics (readers of Ruskin)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for representing mountains, hills, rocks, and foreground soil in landscape painting — how to render mass, detail, light, geological truth, and local individuality. Aimed at helping painters achieve faithful grandeur and convincing small-scale truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad and bold simplicity of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The broad and bold simplicity of mass which influences acting on an enormous scale must inevitably produce in all mountain groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render mountain masses as unified, harmonious wholes — large, simple contours that read as great surges or unified lines (Turner's mountains are given as exemplary). The artist should show the dominant, overarching lines of the group rather than isolated, petty heaps; avoid disconnected, conflicting, 'petty and paltry' mounds as in ancient art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite multiplicity of detail within unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive complication of details accompanies the simplicity of contour: every inch will have its touch of separate character, peculiar curve, melting into the common line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While preserving simple mass, populate surfaces with innumerable subtle local forms and details so the mass still reads as large while the eye finds endless variety (Turner's practice). Group details into larger divisions felt by aerial perspective and personal instants of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association and unity of individual mountain parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Each individual part, being compelled to assume the same symmetrical curves as its neighbors, falls in with their prevailing lines and becomes part of a great and harmonious whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear the structural relationship among eminences: show they were once united and have been divided, so ravines and promontories feel like parts of one system rather than isolated objects. Use continuity of curve and slope to indicate this sympathy of lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of retiring surface / horizontal distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every exhibition of horizontal distance between observer and summit is an addition to height and impressiveness; nature expresses retiring surface by subdued slopes rather than steep, sudden angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor lines of subdued slope and gradual gradation of surface to convey retiring space. Avoid aggressive steepness which diminishes perceived distance and elevation. Turner achieves retiring space by painting surface details (without relying on crossing shadows or artifice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of slope in higher hills
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in lifted masses of enormous mountain the artist should be cautious in the use of violent slopes or vertical lines and studied in the expression of retiring surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making ascents appear abrupt; let the climb be felt as long stretch rather than steep effort. Use delicate gradations so viewers are carried through distance rather than stopped by sudden slopes (Skiddaw and Fort Augustus cited as models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity and limited scale of precipices among secondary hills
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for the slope of a mountain (not actually a precipice of rock) to exceed about 35°–40° among secondary hills; precipices rising vertically more than 100 feet are very rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-emphasize or invent vast vertical cliffs in secondary hillscapes; peaks and precipices should appear as jags or steps emerging from great curves and balanced by long intervals of gentler ascent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of aerial perspective to group multiplicities
rubrics_metrics.description: All multiplicity will be grouped into larger divisions, each felt by their increasing aerial perspective and their instants of individual form, these into larger, until all are merged in the great impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aerial perspective (fading, softening, and relative tones) to organize scales: small details recede into medium groups which recede into the principal dynasties of the scene. This gives hierarchical sense of scale and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to geological truth in large and small features
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense observation and strict adherence to truth in large things (and likely in small) — paintings might illustrate a lecture on the physical sciences; such fidelity underlies the most convincing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study geologic structure and processes (streams cutting ravines, stratification, lamination, etc.) to inform both massing and detail. Even if the painter doesn't 'know' geology technically, their observations should align with geological reality to be convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the ancients' disconnected hill treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient masters' hills are separate, conflicting, confused, petty heaps without marking of distances or divisions; they are invariably diminutive and contemptible in impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject isolated, unassociated hill-heaps. Always indicate valleys, divisions, and the continuous body of the rock so the scene attains grandeur rather than paltriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of river–hill interaction (cutting of bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rivers passing through valleys cut away hill bases, producing precipices and interrupted slopes; this process should be shown so that ravines and promontories feel connected to stream action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint river currents and their effects at bases of hills (shallow/deep sides, cut banks) so hills feel formed by the same forces that shape the valley; use this to justify local precipices and interrupts in slope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular and individual truth over general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so great a sign of truth and beauty as the appearance of individuality — that every inch of mountain must have existence in reality; particular truths are more important than general ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to make forms feel specific and local, as if recognisable to inhabitants; avoid generic, formulaic outlines that read as the artist's invention rather than nature's fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisibility of the artist (let nature seem to have done all)
rubrics_metrics.description: We honor the artist most when we most forget him; he becomes great when he becomes invisible — when one feels that nothing has been imagined or invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and render so the viewer perceives nature rather than the artist's hand: avoid signature mannerisms that call attention to invention; make verisimilitude the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper study method: fresh observation vs studio invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Some artists 'invent hills from possessed stores of knowledge' rather than express fresh ideas received from nature; this makes their work too recognizably their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from direct observation regularly; balance study with continued engagement in nature. Avoid relying solely on past studies or a studio formula (the critique of Stanfield and plea to study local rock types and varied formations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate rendering of rock types and their characteristic fractures
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratified rocks without subdivision (limestones/sandstones) differ from those divided by lamination (slates); rock characters manifest in fractures, obtuse angles, laminae, and convex transitions from light to dark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify rock materials and render their specific cleavage, lamination, and fracture patterns. Show the convex swelling at angles and the stepped truncations caused by weathering and frost (examples: Napoleon in the Academy foreground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness of light, shade, and reflected light on rock
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark sides of fractured stone receive brilliant reflexes from lighted surfaces; every crack and fissure has its shadow and reflected light separated with exquisite precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transparent color and delicate, scientific drawing to separate dark side, shadow, and reflected light clearly. Avoid muddling these into local color or generic gray washes; precision is required to express solid form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express rock hardness and brittleness via slender fissures and sharp lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Few rocks are untraversed by delicate and slender fissures whose black sharp lines are the means by which brittleness is suggested; scars and splinters indicate brittleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include fine fissures, sharp crack-lines and splintery edges in foregounds to convey brittleness and solidity; avoid broad blots or sweeping daubs that suggest malleability or drapery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular, sweeping daubs that make rock like drapery (Salvator's fault)
rubrics_metrics.description: Salvator often gives a concave sweep for the dark side, leaving paint darkest towards the light, resulting in forms like drapery, ribbons, or locks of hair — unlike rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use broad concave sweeps and random stains on rock surfaces. Reject penmanship-like sweeping strokes; prefer angular, varied, and scientifically informed marks that correspond to geological structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity between dark side, shadow, and local color (avoid confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Old masters often confused shadow with dark side and local color; strokes of the brush were dashed without aim beyond covering the canvas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep distinctions clear: the dark side (local form), the cast shadow, and local color must each be handled deliberately. Avoid treating rocks as 'great irregular, formless, characterless lump[s]' with indiscriminate gray marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make mountains a primary subject when appropriate (avoid relegating them to backgrounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an artist makes mountains only backgrounds for foliage or buildings they will miss opportunities; mountains should sometimes be the subject dependent for interest on their forms alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally compose studies where mountain forms are the principal interest to develop facility and conviction in rendering them. This counters tendencies toward thin or incomplete distances when mountains are treated as mere backdrops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice focused studies (dry drawing and chiaroscuro) to improve realization
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists like Copley Fielding lose themselves when removing the veiling mystery; a few thorough studies in clear, strong, front chiaroscuro, allowing neither color nor mist, will open sources of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do hard dry studies and disciplined drawing in strong light to build anatomical and structural knowledge of forms; do not overproduce coloristic works to the neglect of drawing practice. Progress comes from deliberate study, not repetition of unchanging conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render soils and loose earth with furrows and undulating lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A steep bank of loose earth exposed to weather contains features: undulating lines, descents of rain, little ravines cut at the same slope as mountains, leaving graceful ridges chiselled sharply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint soils with small-scale organization analogous to mountains: furrows, rain-cut ravines, and ridges that echo broader hill forms. These details can give high gratification and are governed by rigid laws of organization.
